content: 1. Soiled linen that has been in contact with patients suffering from viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF) should be handled with extreme caution due to the high risk of contamination with bodily fluids such as blood, vomit, or stool. Handling these items may result in splashes, which pose a significant risk of infection. 2. Contaminated linen should be placed in clearly labeled, leak-proof bags or containers at the site of use. The external surfaces of these containers must be disinfected with an effective disinfectant before being removed from the site. 3. Ideally, soiled linen should be incinerated to eliminate any unnecessary risks to individuals handling these materials. 4. If incineration is not possible, the linen should be transported directly to the laundry area and promptly washed with water and detergent. A 0.5% chlorine solution should be used to soak the linen for approximately 15 minutes before laundering. Afterward, the linen should be dried according to standard procedures. 5. Waste management during VHF outbreaks requires careful triaging to ensure safe and appropriate handling of all waste materials. 6. Sharp objects, such as needles, syringes, glass articles, and tubing that have been in contact with the bloodstream, must be disposed of in puncture-resistant containers. These containers should be located as close as possible to the area where the items are used. 7. Solid, non-sharp medical waste should be collected in leak-proof waste bags and covered bins. After each waste load, the waste should be covered with a layer of soil 10–15 cm deep. 8. An incinerator may be used for short periods during an outbreak to destroy solid waste. It is critical to ensure complete incineration of the waste. Caution must be exercised when handling flammable materials and when wearing gloves, as ignited gloves can cause burn injuries. 9. Placenta and anatomical samples should be buried in a separate pit to prevent contamination. 10. The area designated for the final treatment and disposal of waste should have controlled access to prevent entry by animals, untrained personnel, or children. 11. When handling solid infectious waste, individuals should wear heavy-duty gloves, gowns, and closed shoes, such as boots, to minimize exposure risks. 12. Liquid waste, such as feces, urine, vomit, and wastewater from cleaning, can be disposed of in the sanitary sewer or pit latrine without requiring further treatment. 13. When handling liquid infectious waste, such as secretions or excretions containing visible blood, appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) must be worn. This includes gloves, gowns, closed shoes, and facial protection. Care should be taken to avoid splashing during disposal. 14. Goggles provide superior protection against splashes compared to visors, particularly for splashes originating from below when pouring liquid waste from a bucket.
